newsitem.title: ISRAEL: No quick U.S. fix to Middle East crisis - analysts.
newsitem.headline: No quick U.S. fix to Middle East crisis - analysts.

text.p: Bullets flew in the West Bank on Tuesday even before Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu's plane could carry him home from talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton on saving Middle East peace.
Israeli gunfire killed and wounded Palestinians in Hebron where fierce clashes underlined the tough challenge Washington faces forging a deal to stop the fighting and revive the talking.
No quick U.S. fix is likely, with the volatile issues of settlements and terrorism the key elements of any compromise, Israeli and Palestinian analysts said.

"Palestinians were disappointed by the (Netanyahu) visit and the summit because it did not move things forward in terms of Israeli settlement activities," said Palestinian political analyst Ghassan al-Khatib.

"Netanyahu concentrated more in his (Washington) press conference on the fact that the Americans did not put pressure on him concerning settlements and that he will continue building in Jabal Abu Ghneim, in Jerusalem and in settlements in general," he told Reuters.

Clashes have erupted almost daily in the West Bank since Israel broke ground for a Jewish housing project in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18 which Palestinians charged will complete a ring of Israeli settlements on disputed land around the city.
Netanyahu defiantly pledged in Washington that work would continue at the hilltop site Israel calls Har Homa and Arabs call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
"This means that he does not want peace," Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Gaza.
Asked about a possible compromise, Israeli and Palestinian analysts noted that Clinton had yet to disclose the proposals he said he would discuss with the Palestinians this week.
But Gerald Steinberg, of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University near Tel Aviv, predicted the U.S. "package" would hold few surprises.

Under a compromise deal, Arafat would make "very clear statements...that for the first time are going to come out strongly against terrorism in a public way, in Arabic, to his own constituency," Steinberg told Reuters.
Netanyahu has demanded Arafat crack down on Moslem militants as a condition for resuming talks after a March 21 suicide bombing that killed three Israeli women in Tel Aviv.

"I think on the Israeli side, the package will be...something towards a pledge not to start new settlements or not to take actions which are unilateral in areas which are to be negotiated in the final-status (talks)," Steinberg said, referring to negotiations on a final settlement including the future status of Jerusalem.
Khatib said "it should be possible and easy" for Arafat to ease Israeli concerns over Moslem militants through statements or actions on the ground.

"The starting point...is to resume the security coordination through which ideas might be exchanged and measures and policies can be done practically," Khatib said. "But I think the problem is the settlement aspect and the redeployment aspect."
Israel, he said, "cannot simply continue saying 'we will build wherever we want'."
Moreover, Palestinians reject Israel's unilateral determination of the scope of three troop redeployments from mainly rural areas of the West Bank, Khatib said.

The Palestinian Authority spurned Israel's decision to hand over nine percent of the West Bank last month, holding out for three times as much land and a say in the size of the pullbacks due to be completed under an interim peace accord by mid-1998.
Khatib was also dismissive of Netanyahu's proposal to reach a final peace deal with the Palestinians within six months instead of the scheduled two years.

"I don't think that this is serious...the fact the two sides are not able to make progress on these interim, minor things, doesn't give any indicator that the potential for progress on the final issues is easier," he said.
Steinberg forecast more Israeli-Palestinian unrest while U.S. diplomacy gets into gear.
"This was the pattern that was set a few weeks ago and it was very predictable," he said. "I don't expect it to change in the short term. I think the crisis will sharpen."
